correctness.rationale: For \(E_d\), the structure matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&d\end{pmatrix}\) has determinant \(-1\), so \(E_d^2=E_d\) over every field and the derived series never vanishes. Solving \((a e_1+b e_2)^2=a e_1+b e_2\) gives \(a=b^2\) and, for \(b\ne0\), exactly \(d=b^{-1}-b^2\); \(b=0\) forces \(a=0\). Since \(K^\times\) has \(q-1\) elements and \(K\) has \(q\), some \(d\) lies outside that image. The one-dimensional lower bound follows from \(e^2=\lambda e\): \(\lambda=0\) is solvable and \(\lambda\ne0\) gives the idempotent \(\lambda^{-1}e\). No finite experiment is used to infer the general theorem.

value.rationale: The result resolves the finite-field minimum-dimension boundary uniformly: the recent complex theorem has minimum counterexample dimension \(3\), while a cited finite-field exception was known only at \(\mathbb F_3\). The construction works for every finite field, including \(\mathbb F_2\), by a one-line parameter-counting mechanism and gives an exact natural obstruction set. This is a structural field-dependence statement, not a routine recomputation of the \(\mathbb F_3\) example.
